name: Bullying, Cyberbullying, and Deepfakes
title: Bullying, Cyberbullying, and Deepfakes
answer: Bullying now often happens online where adults cannot see it, and AI has added a new harm in the form of fake images and videos of real students. Schools need ways to learn about online cruelty, respond quickly and fairly, and support victims of deepfakes while holding those who create them accountable under the district's code.

sections.body: This idea covers online bullying and the newer harm of deepfakes, meaning fake images or videos of real students. Bullying that moves online is hard for adults to see, follows students home, and can spread quickly, so schools need ways to learn about it and respond. Anonymous reporting tools give students a route to tell adults what is happening, and lessons on digital citizenship help them understand the harm of online cruelty and how to respond when they witness it. AI has added a further problem because a student can use freely available tools to create a fake explicit image of a classmate. The idea solves the gap between harm that happens off school grounds and the school's duty to respond and support victims.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, schools use anonymous reporting tools so students can tell adults about online cruelty, and they teach digital citizenship lessons so students understand the harm and know how to respond when they see it. Adults who respond quickly and fairly to reports build the trust that brings more reports, because students report more when they believe something will happen. Schools should also include deepfakes in their conduct codes and prepare to support victims. When a fake image or video of a student appears, the school should help remove the images, protect the victim from further harm, and connect them with a counselor. Staff should never share or forward the images, even to report them, and discipline for the student who created the image should follow the district's code with attention to the serious harm caused.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports that in a survey of Chinese middle school students, more than a third reported involvement in cyberbullying, and students who were both bullies and victims were at the greatest risk of harm (Li et al., 2023). It also states that online bullying follows students home and can spread quickly. The text notes that students report more when they believe something will happen, which supports the value of quick and fair responses. Beyond these points, the text does not present further research on deepfakes in schools, so that part of the idea rests on practice and on the legal change described in Chapter 3 rather than on school-based studies.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks here are serious. Victims of deepfakes need immediate support, and the school should help remove the images, protect the victim from further harm, and connect them with a counselor. Staff should never share or forward the images, even to report them, because passing them on causes more harm. Discipline for the student who created the image stays with the district's code and should reflect the serious harm caused, so the decision remains with people following that code rather than with any automated tool. The text also notes that the TAKE IT DOWN Act makes knowingly sharing intimate deepfakes a federal crime and requires platforms to remove them quickly, which is a legal matter for the appropriate authorities. Schools should include deepfakes in their conduct codes and prepare to support victims, and the judgment about how to respond stays with staff and district leaders.
